newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Pfizer rides drugs research roller coaster.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Pfizer rides drugs research roller coaster.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
To call it a billion dollar lottery underplays the huge amount of brain-power being deployed by thousands of scientists.
But pharmaceuticals research is a hugely risky business.
Pfizer Inc, the U.S. drugs and healthcare company, spent $1.7 billion on research last year, and expects this to reach $2 billion in 1997.
Pfizer is the sixth biggest drug company in the world in terms of sales. Britain's Glaxo Wellcome is the first followed by Novartis of Switzerland.
ONLY ONE IN 12 DRUGS MAKE IT TO MARKET

The world's top 10 pharmaceutical firms each spend more than $1 billion a year on research. That masks a process which has an attrition rate for potential new products that other industries might find impossible to contemplate.

"For every 12 compounds we put into development, only one actually makes it to the market," said Simon Campbell, head of research at Pfizer's Sandwich facility. "The development time for each of these new drugs is something like 10 or 12 years to get them to people," Campbell told Reuters in an interview.
VIAGRA BREAK
This ruthless process of evaluation and dumping can occasionally lead to lucky breaks.

One drug which appeared to be a not very effective anti-angina treatment, ended up as a highly impressive cure for impotence. The resulting drug Viagra promises to start racking up huge sales in two to three years.
Pfizer employs 1,420 scientists at Sandwich, on the east Kent coast about 70 miles (110 km) from London, out of a worldwide total of 4,500 researchers in Groton, Connecticut, and Nagoya, Japan.
EACH DRUG COSTS AN AVERAGE $500 MILLION TO PRODUCE
Roger Burgess, director of central research, said it costs an average of about $500 million to get each drug to market.

When researchers identify a chemical combination which has disease healing promise, it starts the obstacle course to the consumer. It begins with pre-clinical tests, often in animals, to see if the product is toxic. The compound then enters "phase 1" human toleration tests, "phase 2" safety and dosage measurement, and then "phase 3" long term safety evaluation.
Regulatory authorities then must pore over the research before permission is given for public use.

"When we first discover a potential compound the research teams are ecstatic and we organise a big party. We certainly have another one here," said Burgess, pointing to the end of "phase 3" on a chart, "and boy do we have a party when we get here," he added, as the drug finally gets to the consumer.
PFIZER RESEARCH HIGHLY RATED BY ANALYSTS
Pfizer has a powerful reputation for pharmaceuticals research among independent analysts.

"The Pfizer research pipeline has been prolific and has been enough to maintain one of the highest (sales) growth rates in the industry," said Robert Uhl, pharmaceuticals analyst with merchant bankers Salomon Brothers in New York.
"It is definitely one of the top five in the world in terms of the quality of their research.
"Viagra will be one of the most exciting pharmaceutical products in the next few years," Uhl said.

Since 1995 Pfizer has introduced about half a dozen new products to the market. These include Norvasc, which now has annual sales of about $1.8 billion and lowers blood pressure, and anti-fungal agent Diflucan, selling at nearly $1 billion a year. Cardura treats hypertension. All three were developed at Sandwich.
PFIZER HAS HIGH HOPES OF NEW DRUG PIPELINE
Campbell, who also heads Pfizer's world-wide drug discovery programme, has high hopes for a string of new products which should enter the market by early next century.
"Aricept for Alzheimers and Lipitor to lower cholesterol will be launched this year along with Trovafloxacin, an antibiotic," Campbell said.
Aricept and Lipitor are licensed from other drugs companies.
"When there is a gap in our pipeline we aggressively seek out products to license," Campbell said.
"Then there is Dofetilide, which controls serious heart disrhythmias. After heart attacks many die suddenly because of these problems; this drug stabilises the heart."
Campbell said Dofetilide, pencilled in for rollout by 1999, won't be a blockbuster but meets a pressing medical need.
The anti-schizophrenia product Ziprasidone should also hit markets by 1999.

"Looking further out things become less certain. We're looking at launching in the year 2000 Candoxatril, a Sandwich compound for congestive heart failure, Voriconazole, which attacks a life threatening fungus, and Eletriptan, again from Sandwich, which controls migraine.
"...we hope that Darifenacin...will be launched for treatment of urine incontinence which is very big problem for the elderly, and irritable bowel syndrome."
GENOME PROJECT MAY EVENTUALLY UNLEASH PRODUCT FLOOD
Campbell says biotechnology is a promising area for research, and it plans to continue collaboration with smaller biotech companies, rather than seeking to acquire them.
"We are investing up to $100 million a year in new technologies and genome sciences," Campbell said.
The human genome project, a worldwide enterprise to map and sequence the human genetic code, promises a great leap forward in treatments for previously incurable diseases.
"It will take time to evaluate the function of all the genes, but when we do the gates might open and a whole flood of new products come out.

"I'd like to say that great diseases will go. At the moment we are treating disease rather than actually curing. We will be able to gene-type people and see if they are susceptible to diseases. If you don't have a cure though it's a moot point whether we want to know that in say three years we have a one in three chance of heart failure."
